dimoose: readiness for rOpenSci software peer review

Source: ropensci-readiness.md

Status: nothing has been submitted. No pre-submission inquiry, review request or issue has been opened with rOpenSci or anywhere else. This is a working document for the maintainer, and the inquiry at the end is a draft.

An audit of dimoose against the rOpenSci Dev Guide.

  • Updated 19 November 2026 for the uncommitted working tree that becomes version 0.3.0: the rows marked (0.3.0) below were re-read against that tree. The measured figures (check status, test counts, coverage) were not re-measured; they are still those of commit 1831f44.

  • Audited: version 0.2.0 at commit 1831f44, plus the files added with this audit (.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml, .github/workflows/test-coverage.yaml, codemeta.json, CONTRIBUTING.md, inst/CITATION, webr/). Work in progress in the working tree on other files was not audited.

  • Sources (fetched 2026-11-19): Packaging guide, Continuous integration, Policies: aims and scope, Guide for authors, and the pre-submission and submission issue templates.

  • Measured locally (macOS, R 4.6.1, on a clean export of the commit, with NOT_CRAN=false and no Python configured, as on CI): R CMD check --no-manual gives Status: OK; tests FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 9 | PASS 888; covr reports 92.4% line coverage. Linux and Windows results will only be known when the new workflow first runs on GitHub.

  • Not run: pkgcheck::pkgcheck() (not installed here). Editors run it on every submission, so run it before submitting; see “Before submitting” below.

Summary

The package is in good technical shape for review: it passes R CMD check cleanly, has a large test suite with high coverage, a pkgdown site, four vignettes and roxygen2 documentation. The open points, most important first:

  1. Scope. Not an obvious fit; needs a pre-submission inquiry (draft below). The reading, checking, pruning and publishing of keys fits, and 0.3.0 makes that core much larger (plain-text keys, SDD, DELTA, Lucid and Xper, regional keys). The machine-learning parts probably do not fit; the mixed-effects trees have moved to a companion package, mecit.
  2. Naming. Functions are camelCase; rOpenSci strongly recommends snake_case. A discussion point for the inquiry, not something to change first.
  3. Examples. About 20 exported functions have no example.
  4. README. Now has CI and coverage badges, a citation line, a short related-software section and a link to CONTRIBUTING.md (0.3.0). Still missing: a repostatus badge and a code of conduct.
  5. Live web tests are skipped on CI, where the guide wants them to run.
  6. Licence is now GPL (>= 3) (0.3.0); there is still no licence file in the repository.

Scope fit

The closest categories, with what in the package supports each:

  • data munging (best fit): “tools for handling data in specific scientific formats”. An identification key is such a format, and the package’s core is representing keys (dimoose, keyFromLeads()), validating them (key$validate()), and converting them (toNewick(), toTreedata(), toIgraph(), toAuspiceJSON(), readHaplogrep(), haplotypeMatrix()).
  • data retrieval: importFishbase() downloads and parses FishBase keys; checkNames() checks names against the GBIF backbone.
  • field and laboratory reproducibility tools: “form and data sheet generation” for field protocols. keyFromSpreadsheet() + exportWizard() + keyDiagram() turn a key kept in a spreadsheet into an offline phone page and a printable diagram.
  • data validation and testing: key$validate() and checkNames(), a smaller part.

Likely to be judged out of scope:

  • Keys generated by modelling: generateTree(), keyFromRpart(), keyFromMatrix(), keyFromAlignment(), and the photo pipeline (visionModel(), embedImages(), discoverSniglets(), keyFromSniglets(), keyFromClusters(), identifyPhotos()). The data-extraction category says “statistical/ML libraries for modelling or prediction are typically not included”. These could instead fall under the statistical software track (Machine Learning; Dimensionality Reduction, Clustering and Unsupervised Learning), which has its own standards and requires srr annotations.
  • mecit(), keyFromMecit() and simulateExpression() are no longer part of dimoose (0.3.0): they moved to the companion package mecit.
  • keyDiagram(): “data visualization packages are no longer in scope”, though here it is an export of the key rather than general plotting.

Editors may ask for the package to be split (for example a core key package and a dimoose.vision companion). Decide beforehand whether that would be acceptable; the inquiry draft below asks the question openly.

Before submitting

In this order:

  1. Push the workflows, add CODECOV_TOKEN, and get all five check jobs green. The 0.3.0 tree has not been through R CMD check on any platform.
  2. Regenerate codemeta.json with codemetar (the licence is now explicit; the file was corrected by hand).
  3. Add a code of conduct and, when you are ready to call the package active, the repostatus badge. Search for related R packages and extend the README’s related-software section. (Badges, citation line and the section itself are in.)
  4. Add the missing examples. (The package-level help page is rewritten.)
  5. Decide how the live web tests should run on CI (recorded responses or a scheduled job).
  6. Install and run pkgcheck::pkgcheck() and fix or explain what it reports; the submission form asks for the reasons for any failing item.
  7. Open the pre-submission inquiry below, and wait for the editors’ answer on scope and naming before spending time on a rename or a split.

Draft pre-submission inquiry

To be posted by the maintainer at https://github.com/ropensci/software-review/issues/new/choose using the “Submit a presubmission inquiry” template, which this follows. It is a draft: check every statement, and complete the places marked TODO.

Submitting Author Name: Jeremy Leipzig Submitting Author Github Handle: @leipzig Repository: https://github.com/leipzig/dimoose Submission type: Pre-submission Language: en

  • Paste the full DESCRIPTION file inside a code block below:
(paste DESCRIPTION here at the time of posting)

Scope

  • Please indicate which category or categories this package falls under:

    Data Lifecycle Packages

  • Explain how and why the package falls under these categories (briefly, 1-2 sentences). Please note any areas you are unsure of:

    dimoose handles one scientific data type, the dichotomous identification key: it reads keys from plain text, a spreadsheet, FishBase and the exchange formats of other key software (SDD, DELTA, Lucid, Xper), checks them (dead ends, unreachable couplets, species names against the GBIF backbone), cuts them down to the taxa recorded in a region, converts them to tree formats used in phylogenetics (Newick, treedata, igraph, Auspice JSON), and writes them out as a self-contained offline web page or a diagram for use in the field.

    I am unsure about two things. First, the package also generates keys from data: from a character matrix, from a sequence alignment and from photo embeddings (CLIP/BioCLIP through reticulate or ONNX Runtime). I expect these to be outside the data-lifecycle categories, and would like to know whether you would prefer them split into a separate package, reviewed under the statistical software track, or left in and excluded from review. Second, exported functions are camelCase (keyFromSpreadsheet(), exportWizard()). I would like to know whether a move to snake_case would be a condition of acceptance before I plan a deprecation cycle.

  • If submitting a statistical package, have you already incorporated documentation of standards into your code via the srr package?

    No. This is not submitted as a statistical package; see the question above.

  • Who is the target audience and what are scientific applications of this package?

    Taxonomists, field biologists, naturalists and teachers who write or maintain identification keys, and people who compile them into regional guides. A key kept in a spreadsheet becomes a checked, versionable object, and the same source produces the phone wizard, the printed diagram and the tree file. Researchers working with decision-tree-like structures in other fields can use the same object, for example the human mitochondrial haplogroup tree (PhyloTree Build 17 is included).

  • Are there other R packages that accomplish the same thing? If so, how does yours differ or meet our criteria for best-in-category?

    TODO: confirm with a search of CRAN and R-universe before posting. As far as I know there is no R package for representing, validating and publishing dichotomous keys. rfishbase (rOpenSci) gives access to FishBase tables but, as far as I know, not to its identification keys; taxize resolves names but has no key structure. Interactive key software exists outside R (Lucid, Xper3, DELTA/Intkey); dimoose differs in being scriptable and open source, and in producing a single offline HTML file.

  • (If applicable) Does your package comply with our guidance around Ethics, Data Privacy and Human Subjects Research?

    The package collects no personal data. The bundled human mitochondrial tree is a published phylogeny of haplogroups, not data about individuals.

  • Any other questions or issues we should be aware of?

    importFishbase() reads FishBase’s public key pages (HTML), sending an identifying user agent. TODO: state what FishBase’s terms of use say about this once checked. The photo-based features need Python, which reticulate installs on first use; they are optional and their tests are skipped on CI.

Use of Generative AI

  • TODO: describe in your own words. The Git history records AI assistance in commit trailers (Co-Authored-By: Claude ...), and the CI workflows, CONTRIBUTING.md, codemeta.json, inst/CITATION, the webr/ page and this readiness audit were drafted with Claude Code and should be reviewed by you before submission.
